name: Drug Policy Alliance (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: people in the United States spared drug arrests, overdose deaths averted, and cannabis users (New York, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon).
summary: Drug Policy Alliance is the largest US group campaigning to end the war on drugs (12.2 million dollars spent by the 501(c)(3) in the year to May 2025; its 501(c)(4), Drug Policy Action, isn't tax-deductible and isn't counted). Its spending over fiscal years 2021-2025 is counted as a past average over the wins of those years: a share of marijuana legalisation in New York, New Jersey and New Mexico (about 40,000 possession arrests a year ended, about 760,000 records cleared and users' gains from legal supply, less the rise in cannabis use disorder legalisation brings), a small share of New York City's overdose prevention centres and other harm-reduction laws (deaths averted), and a small share of Oregon's Measure 110 while it was in force (arrests ended, less the overdose deaths one study attributes to it); every branch is discounted for missing data. The result is about 0.001 years of healthy life per 1,000 dollars, far below the median of the site's global-health models: arrests weigh little on a scale set by deaths, legalisation's health cost nearly cancels its gains, and DPA's share of each coalition is small. The result is mostly uncertainty, from below zero to about ten times the best guess; the biggest unknowns are how much legalisation raises cannabis use disorder and what legal supply and cleared records are worth to people.

source.title: charityevals' estimate: Drug Policy Alliance

sections.title: Cost
sections.explainer: What the modelled program cost in the year the outcomes below are counted for, including its share of overhead. From audited financial statements or the annual report.

sections.title: Reach
sections.explainer: How many people, animals or meals the spending reached in the same year, as the charity reports it.

sections.title: Effect per unit
sections.explainer: What the intervention does for each unit reached, from the best available studies, before any adjustment.

sections.title: Adjustments
sections.explainer: Discounts for weaker evidence, what would have happened anyway, credit shared with others, and delivery falling short. All multiply the outcome.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.explainer: The outcome in the family's shared unit, per dollar.

sections.title: Your dollar's share
sections.explainer: Staff who earn less than they could elsewhere pay part of the cost in kind. With credit by share of resources, your dollar is credited with its share of the full cost only.

rows.label: Overdoses reversed a year at the New York City centres
rows.explainer: The four-year count spread evenly.

rows.label: Deaths averted per overdose reversed at a centre

source.title: Milloy et al. (2008), Estimated Drug Overdose Deaths Averted by North America's First Medically-Supervised Safer Injection Facility, PLoS ONE 3(10): e3351
source.quote: the estimates of the number of prevented deaths ranged from eight to 51

rows.explainer: Not every overdose at a centre would have killed: many would have been witnessed or reversed elsewhere. Milloy et al. (2008) estimated 8 to 51 deaths averted from Vancouver's 1,004 overdose events at Insite (0.8% to 5.1%), before fentanyl, which makes an unattended overdose more often fatal. Our judgment: 3% (1% to 10%).

rows.label: Other harm-reduction wins of the period, as a multiple of the New York centres' deaths averted

source.title: Drug Policy Alliance, 2024 Year in Review
source.quote: Passing legislation to establish overdose prevention centers in Vermont

rows.explainer: DPA also won or helped win Rhode Island's 2021 law for harm-reduction centres (Providence's centre opened in late 2024), Vermont's 2024 law for a Burlington centre (passed over the governor's veto; not yet open by May 2025), California's 2024 law decriminalising and expanding drug checking for fentanyl and xylazine, and test-strip laws in other states (DPA 2024 Year in Review). Most are smaller or later than New York's centres, and drug checking's effect on deaths is unmeasured. Our judgment: half the New York centres' deaths averted (0.15 to 1.5).

rows.label: Overdose deaths averted a year by the period's harm-reduction wins
rows.explainer: Reversals times the deaths each averts, plus the other wins.

rows.label: Years from the period's start until the centres' deaths averted begin
rows.explainer: The New York centres opened 17 months into the period (June 2020 to November 2021); Rhode Island's and the drug-checking laws came later. Our judgment: 1.5 years (0.5 to 3).

rows.label: Harm reduction: discounted years counted
rows.explainer: The shared years a won reform counts, discounted at the shared rate after the wait.

rows.label: Harm reduction: value of the deaths averted, per year of spending
rows.explainer: Deaths averted a year, valued by age, over the years counted, spread over the five years of spending.

rows.label: New York: marijuana possession arrests a year ended by legalisation (March 2021)

source.title: NORML, New York Marijuana Arrests (state marijuana arrest reports, from the FBI's NIBRS data)

rows.explainer: New York's possession arrests fell from 33,347 in 2019 (when a first law made small amounts a violation) and 19,413 in 2020 to 583 in 2021 and 474 in 2022 after the Marijuana Regulation and Taxation Act (FBI NIBRS via NORML, which undercounts). The 2020 level, partly pandemic, against the 2019 one: 15,000 a year (8,000 to 25,000).

rows.label: New Jersey: marijuana possession arrests a year ended by legalisation (February 2021)

source.title: NORML, New Jersey Marijuana Arrests (state marijuana arrest reports, from the FBI's NIBRS data)

rows.explainer: New Jersey's possession arrests: 28,865 in 2019, 19,911 in 2020 (pandemic), 200 in 2021 and 118 in 2022 after the legalisation and decriminalisation laws of February 2021 (FBI NIBRS via NORML). 25,000 a year (18,000 to 29,000).

rows.label: New Mexico: marijuana possession arrests a year ended by legalisation (June 2021)

source.title: NORML, New Mexico Marijuana Arrests (state marijuana arrest reports, from the FBI's NIBRS data)

rows.explainer: New Mexico made small amounts a civil fine in July 2019: 1,447 possession arrests in 2019, 328 in 2020 (FBI NIBRS via NORML); the Cannabis Regulation Act ended the rest. 300 a year (150 to 1,000).

rows.label: Marijuana possession arrests a year ended in the three states
rows.explainer: The sum of the three states.

rows.label: Days in custody per marijuana possession arrest
rows.explainer: Most possession arrests ended in a desk appearance ticket or release within hours; some were held overnight for arraignment, and a few, with warrants or other charges, longer. Our judgment: half a day (0.1 to 2).

rows.label: Other harm of a possession arrest, in days of custody's life-satisfaction cost
rows.explainer: Court dates, fines and fees, lost work and the fear and stigma of an arrest, before any lasting record (counted below). Our judgment: as much life satisfaction as 3 days in custody (0.5 to 15).

rows.label: Years from the period's start until the arrests stopped

source.title: Drug Policy Alliance press release, It's official: governor signs New York marijuana legalization (31 March 2021, Common Dreams newswire copy)
source.quote: Through its Start SMART NY campaign, DPA has worked to end marijuana prohibition in New York

rows.explainer: The three laws were signed in February to April 2021 and possession was legal at once in New York and New Jersey, from June 2021 in New Mexico: about 0.75 years into the period (0.5 to 1.2).

rows.label: Legalisation: discounted years counted
rows.explainer: The shared years a won reform counts, discounted after the wait.

rows.label: Legalisation: life satisfaction kept by people not arrested, per year of spending
rows.explainer: Arrests ended times their custody and other harm, priced at the shared life-satisfaction cost of a year inside, over the years counted, spread over the five years of spending.

rows.label: Legalisation: deaths averted by less time in custody, per year of spending
rows.formula: can_arrests_per_year * can_custody_days_per_arrest / 365 * custody_deaths_per_year * custody_value_per_death * can_discounted_years / campaign_years
rows.explainer: The custody days avoided times the shared deaths per year in short custody, valued at the ages of people arrested.

rows.label: New York: past marijuana convictions sealed or expunged by the 2021 law

source.title: NORML, New York: Officials Moving to Clear Over 400,000 Past Marijuana Convictions (22 October 2021)
source.quote: Officials Moving to Clear Over 400,000 Past Marijuana Convictions

rows.explainer: New York's Office of Cannabis Management said in October 2021 that nearly 200,000 convictions were already sealed and several hundred thousand more being expunged automatically under the law: about 400,000 (300,000 to 450,000).

rows.label: New Jersey: marijuana cases expunged under the 2021 law

source.title: New Jersey Courts, Marijuana record expungement
source.quote: expunged more than 362,000 marijuana and hashish cases

rows.explainer: The New Jersey courts expunged more than 362,000 marijuana and hashish cases from court records after the decriminalisation law took effect on 1 July 2021.

rows.label: Gain in ln(income) a year for a person whose marijuana record is cleared
rows.explainer: People who petition to clear a conviction earn markedly more afterwards (Prescott and Starr 2020, Michigan: wages up 22% within two years), but they are selected; automatic clearance of old low-level records, many held by people with other records or long past any job search, shows little effect on employment in the studies of it. Our judgment: 0.2% (0 to 1%) a year.

rows.label: Years a cleared record's gain lasts
rows.explainer: Our judgment: 5 years (2 to 10), as old records matter less over time.

rows.label: Legalisation: income gained by clearing records, per year of spending
rows.formula: (can_records_ny + can_records_nj) * can_record_ln_gain * $uov_per_ln_consumption * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, can_record_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - can_years_until_effect) / campaign_years
rows.explainer: Records cleared (a one-off, not a yearly flow) times the yearly gain over its discounted years, after the wait, spread over the five years of spending.

rows.label: Population of New York, New Jersey and New Mexico (2020 Census)

source.title: US Census Bureau, 2020 Census Apportionment Results, Table 2: resident population by state
source.quote: New York 20,201,249; New Jersey 9,288,994; New Mexico 2,117,522

rows.explainer: Residents of the three states: 20,201,249, 9,288,994 and 2,117,522.

rows.label: Share of the population aged 26 or older
rows.explainer: Our judgment, anchored on the national age profile (about 22% of Americans under 18 and about 12% aged 18 to 25 in the 2020 Census), which the three states are close to: 66% (63% to 69%).

rows.label: Share of the population aged 12 to 17
rows.explainer: Our judgment, anchored on the national age profile (six single years of age at about 1.25% of the population each): 7.5% (7% to 8%).

rows.label: Past-year cannabis use disorder, adults 26 or older, before legalisation

source.title: Cerdá et al. (2020), Association Between Recreational Marijuana Legalization in the United States and Changes in Marijuana Use and Cannabis Use Disorder From 2008 to 2016, JAMA Psychiatry 77(2): 165-171

rows.explainer: National Survey on Drug Use and Health, states enacting legal sales, before enactment (Cerdá et al. 2020).

rows.label: Odds ratio of cannabis use disorder after legalisation, adults 26 or older

source.title: Cerdá et al. (2020), Association Between Recreational Marijuana Legalization in the United States and Changes in Marijuana Use and Cannabis Use Disorder From 2008 to 2016, JAMA Psychiatry 77(2): 165-171

rows.explainer: The before-after change in states that legalised against the change elsewhere (Cerdá et al. 2020), with its 95% interval.

rows.label: Past-year cannabis use disorder, ages 12 to 17, before legalisation

source.title: Cerdá et al. (2020), Association Between Recreational Marijuana Legalization in the United States and Changes in Marijuana Use and Cannabis Use Disorder From 2008 to 2016, JAMA Psychiatry 77(2): 165-171
source.quote: past-year CUD increased from 2.18% to 2.72% after RML enactment

rows.explainer: As above, for adolescents.

rows.label: Odds ratio of cannabis use disorder after legalisation, ages 12 to 17

source.title: Cerdá et al. (2020), Association Between Recreational Marijuana Legalization in the United States and Changes in Marijuana Use and Cannabis Use Disorder From 2008 to 2016, JAMA Psychiatry 77(2): 165-171
source.quote: a 25% higher increase than that for the same age group in states that did not enact RML (odds ratio [OR], 1.25; 95% CI, 1.01-1.55)

rows.explainer: Cerdá et al. 2020, with its 95% interval; no change was found at 18 to 25.

rows.label: Share of survey-measured cannabis use disorder that is dependence as the Global Burden of Disease counts it
rows.explainer: The survey counts abuse or dependence (DSM-IV); GBD's disability weight is for dependence. Our judgment: 60% (40% to 80%).

rows.label: How far the use-disorder rise is caused by legalisation
rows.explainer: Cerdá et al.'s adolescent result is sensitive to small unmeasured confounding (their own test); the adult one is more robust. A twin study in Colorado and Minnesota found more use but no more disorder symptoms after legalisation, and a difference-in-differences study of mental health found no average effect (harm below 35, improvement above). Two of the three designs find no harm on average, the third a clear rise in disorder. Our judgment: a third of the measured rise (10% to 100%).

rows.label: Legalisation: healthy years lost to more cannabis use disorder, per year of spending
rows.formula: can_population * (can_share_26plus * can_cud_base_26plus * (can_cud_or_26plus - 1) + can_share_12_17 * can_cud_base_12_17 * (can_cud_or_12_17 - 1)) * can_dependence_share * @gbd_disability_weights.cannabis_dependence_average * can_health_evidence_adj * can_discounted_years / campaign_years
rows.explainer: Extra cases (the base rate times the odds ratio less one, for adults and adolescents) times the dependence share and GBD's average disability weight for cannabis dependence (facts/gbd_disability_weights.json), over the years counted, spread over the five years of spending.

rows.label: Past-month cannabis users, share of adults 26 or older after legalisation

source.title: Cerdá et al. (2020), Association Between Recreational Marijuana Legalization in the United States and Changes in Marijuana Use and Cannabis Use Disorder From 2008 to 2016, JAMA Psychiatry 77(2): 165-171
source.quote: past-month marijuana use after RML enactment increased from 5.65% to 7.10%

rows.explainer: 7.10% after legalisation in the states that legalised (Cerdá et al. 2020).

rows.label: Gain in ln(consumption) a year for an adult user from legal supply
rows.explainer: Legal, tested products, no risk of arrest for buying, and, as markets mature, lower prices: if worth about a tenth of what a regular user spends (a few hundred dollars a year against consumption of about 58,000 dollars per person), 0.2% of consumption; New York's legal market opened slowly and legal prices stayed above illicit ones. Our judgment: 0.2% (0 to 0.6%).

rows.label: Legalisation: users' gain from legal supply, per year of spending
rows.formula: can_population * can_share_26plus * can_user_share * can_user_ln_gain * $uov_per_ln_consumption * can_discounted_years / campaign_years
rows.explainer: Adult users times their gain over the years counted, spread over the five years of spending.

source.quote: The number dropped to roughly 3,800 arrests in the same 18-month period after Measure 110 took effect.

source.quote: in the same 18-month period

rows.explainer: Possession had been mostly a misdemeanour since 2017; an arrest brought booking, sometimes days of pretrial jail, and jail sanctions on probation. Our judgment: 3 days (0.5 to 15).

source.quote: Oregon's legislature recriminalized drug possession in March 2024, to take effect in September 2024
source.note: and: Measure 110 took effect in Oregon on February 1, 2021

rows.label: Years from the period's start until Measure 110 took effect

source.title: Zoorob et al. (2024), Drug Decriminalization, Fentanyl, and Fatal Overdoses in Oregon, JAMA Network Open 7(9): e2431612
source.quote: Measure 110 took effect in Oregon on February 1, 2021

rows.explainer: June 2020 to 1 February 2021.

rows.label: Measure 110: discounted years in force
rows.explainer: The years in force, discounted at the shared rate after the wait.

rows.label: Measure 110: life satisfaction kept by people not arrested, per year of spending
rows.explainer: As for marijuana arrests, over the years in force.

rows.label: Measure 110: deaths averted by less time in custody, per year of spending
rows.formula: m110_arrests_per_year * m110_custody_days_per_arrest / 365 * custody_deaths_per_year * custody_value_per_death * m110_discounted_years / campaign_years
rows.explainer: Custody days avoided times the shared deaths per year in short custody.

rows.label: Extra overdose deaths a year attributed to Measure 110 by the one study that finds them

source.title: Spencer (2023), Does drug decriminalization increase unintentional drug overdose deaths? Evidence from Oregon's Measure 110, Journal of Health Economics 91: 102798
source.quote: 182 additional unintentional drug overdose deaths
source.note: as quoted by Zoorob et al. 2024; the working paper gave 181

rows.explainer: Spencer (2023, synthetic control): 182 more unintentional overdose deaths in Oregon in 2021, 23% above the prediction without decriminalisation. The range (120 to 250) is our reading of a one-state synthetic control's precision, as the interval isn't quoted; whether the deaths were caused at all is the next row.

rows.label: Share of that rise caused by decriminalisation

source.title: Zoorob et al. (2024), Drug Decriminalization, Fentanyl, and Fatal Overdoses in Oregon, JAMA Network Open 7(9): e2431612
source.quote: no association between M110 and fatal overdose rates was observed

rows.explainer: Zoorob et al. (2024) replicate Spencer's estimate and find it shrinks to zero once fentanyl's arrival in Oregon is accounted for; Joshi et al. (2023, JAMA Psychiatry) also find no association. Our judgment: 15% of it (0 to 50%).

rows.label: People spared a drug arrest a year by the period's wins
rows.explainer: Marijuana arrests ended in three states plus Oregon's possession arrests (for reading; each branch counts its own).

rows.label: Illness averted per person per year (direct DALYs)
rows.explainer: 0: illness enters only through the use-disorder side effect of legalisation, counted in its own row.

rows.label: Income gain per person per year
rows.explainer: 0: income enters through the cleared records and users' gains, counted in their own rows.

rows.label: Chance the wins counted happen
rows.explainer: The wins counted are in; DPA's share of each is its attribution share.

rows.label: Wait until the wins take effect (outcome-weighted, for reading)
rows.explainer: The branches' waits weighted by their value before adjustments, for reading only: each branch applies its own.

rows.label: The wait, discounted (for reading)
rows.explainer: The wait above at the shared rate.

rows.label: Discounted years counted (for reading)
rows.explainer: The shared years at the outcome-weighted wait, for reading only.

rows.label: People freed by casework
rows.explainer: 0: DPA doesn't take individual cases; its legal team drafts laws and joins cases that set precedent.

rows.label: Detention avoided per person freed
rows.explainer: 0: no casework (above).

rows.label: Life-satisfaction gap between detention and release
rows.explainer: The shared figure, unused without casework.

rows.label: Wellbeing per person freed
rows.explainer: The person's own years, discounted at the shared rate (a release isn't a won reform).

rows.label: Harm reduction: evidence
rows.explainer: The reversals are the operator's own count and the other wins are judged; the deaths each reversal averts is already a judgment with its own range. Our judgment: 85% (60% to 100%), as for Prison Policy Initiative's state wins.

rows.label: Harm reduction: what would have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the shared years counted (or, for Measure 110, its years in force) already say the change would have come, or ended, some day (Convention 5).

rows.label: Harm reduction: DPA's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: The centres are paid for and run by OnPoint NYC (entirely from non-government funds for the consumption rooms) and were sanctioned by the city's health department under Mayor de Blasio; VOCAL-NY, Housing Works and the SIF NYC coalition campaigned beside DPA, which had pressed for them since about 2016. The resources behind the deaths averted are mostly the centres' running costs. Our judgment: 5% (2% to 15%).

rows.label: Harm reduction: delivery
rows.explainer: 1: counted from what happened after the win (arrests that stopped, reversals at open centres), so delivery is already in the counts.

rows.label: Harm reduction: missing-data discount
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): the effect per win rests on judgment and on studies of other places, not on measurement of DPA's own results.

rows.label: Harm reduction: all adjustments
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Legalisation: evidence
rows.explainer: Arrest counts come from FBI incident data that undercount (NORML's caveat), and the harm per arrest is our judgment. Our judgment: 80% (60% to 100%).

rows.label: Legalisation: what would have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the shared years counted (or, for Measure 110, its years in force) already say the change would have come, or ended, some day (Convention 5).

rows.label: Legalisation: DPA's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: DPA ran the Start SMART NY campaign and coalition for the New York law, helped draft and pass New Mexico's (its own press releases), and pressed New Jersey's decriminalisation and expungement terms after the 2020 ballot question its sister 501(c)(4)'s allies ran; VOCAL-NY, the NYCLU, Citizen Action, the cannabis industry's lobbyists and the governors' budget drives carried the same laws, and the c4's own spending isn't in the cost here. Our judgment: 15% (5% to 30%).

rows.label: Legalisation: delivery
rows.explainer: 1: counted from what happened after the win (arrests that stopped, reversals at open centres), so delivery is already in the counts.

rows.label: Legalisation: missing-data discount
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): the effect per win rests on judgment and on studies of other places, not on measurement of DPA's own results.

rows.label: Legalisation: all adjustments
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Measure 110: evidence
rows.explainer: The arrest counts are official; the harm per arrest is our judgment. Our judgment: 80% (60% to 100%).

rows.label: Measure 110: what would have happened anyway
rows.explainer: 1: the shared years counted (or, for Measure 110, its years in force) already say the change would have come, or ended, some day (Convention 5).

rows.label: Measure 110: DPA's share of the resources behind it
rows.explainer: Measure 110 was put on the ballot and paid for by a campaign committee funded mostly by Drug Policy Action, the 501(c)(4), and Dr. Bronner's; the c3 counted here worked on its drafting, implementation and defence (DPA says it prevented full repeal in 2024 and protected funding for services) beside Oregon's Health Justice Recovery Alliance. Our judgment: 8% (2% to 20%).

rows.label: Measure 110: delivery
rows.explainer: 1: counted from what happened after the win (arrests that stopped, reversals at open centres), so delivery is already in the counts.

rows.label: Measure 110: missing-data discount
rows.explainer: The shared missing-data step (docs/normalization.md 2.12): the effect per win rests on judgment and on studies of other places, not on measurement of DPA's own results.

rows.label: Measure 110: all adjustments
rows.explainer: The product of the branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Side effect: families spared a member's arrest and custody, as a share of the arrest branches' value
rows.explainer: The shared share of incarceration's value that falls on partners and children (facts/incarceration.json, Wakefield and Wildeman 2013), applied to the arrests ended.

rows.label: Side effect: infections averted and people brought to treatment by the centres, as a share of the harm-reduction branch
rows.explainer: The New York centres also hand out sterile supplies, test for HIV and hepatitis C and connected about 7,000 people to other care in four years (OnPoint); studies near OnPoint found no rise in crime (Chalfin et al. 2023). Our judgment: 5% of the deaths averted's value (0 to 20%).

rows.label: Side effect: healthy years lost to more cannabis use disorder after legalisation (DPA's share)
rows.explainer: The use-disorder row above, with the legalisation branch's adjustments, entered as a loss.

rows.label: Side effect: users' gain from legal supply (DPA's share)
rows.explainer: The users' gain above, with the legalisation branch's adjustments.

rows.label: Side effect: overdose deaths Measure 110 may have caused (DPA's share)
rows.formula: 0 - m110_od_deaths_spencer * m110_od_evidence * od_value_per_death * m110_discounted_years / campaign_years * m110_total_adj
rows.explainer: Spencer's extra deaths times the share caused by decriminalisation, for each year in force, valued at the ages of US overdose deaths, with the branch's adjustments, entered as a loss.

Not counted: Measure 110's treatment money (cannabis tax moved from other public uses, with no measured gain in outcomes yet) and the stalled decriminalisation campaigns elsewhere after its repeal (a lost future gain, not a harm).
